claim: The spherical stimulus arena contains 14,848 individual LEDs covering over 90% of the visual field of zebrafish larvae.
source: By combining 3D printing with electronic solutions developed in Drosophila vision research, we constructed a spherical stimulus arena containing 14,848 individual LEDs covering over 90% of the visual field of zebrafish larvae (Figure 1c, Materials and methods section on coverage).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of LEDs and coverage percentage, with reference to a figure and methods section.

claim: Zebrafish larvae exhibit optokinetic response (OKR) behavior where eye movements track stimulus motion to minimize retinal slip.
source: When presented with a horizontal moving stimulus pattern, zebrafish larvae exhibit optokinetic response (OKR) behaviour, where eye movements track stimulus motion to minimise retinal slip.
evidence: Figure 1a caption explicitly describes OKR behavior in zebrafish larvae.

claim: The optokinetic response consists of reflexively executed stereotypical eye movements with phases of stimulus 'tracking' (slow phase) interrupted by quick phases.
source: The optokinetic response (OKR) consists of reflexively executed stereotypical eye movements, in which phases of stimulus 'tracking' (slow phase) are interrupted by quick phases (Figure 1a).
evidence: The manuscript directly describes the components of OKR behavior.

claim: In the quick phases of OKR, eye position is reset by a saccade in the direction opposite to stimulus motion.
source: In the quick phases, eye position is reset by a saccade in the direction opposite to stimulus motion.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the mechanism of quick phases.

claim: The visual field of individual 4-day-old zebrafish larvae has been reported to cover about 163° per eye.
source: Zebrafish are lateral-eyed animals and have a large visual field, which increases during early development and in individual 4-day-old larvae has been reported to cover about 163° per eye (Easter and Nicola, 1996), although little is known about interindividual variability.
evidence: The claim cites a specific study (Easter and Nicola, 1996) for the visual field measurement.

claim: Zebrafish retina contains four different cone photoreceptor types.
source: Their retina contains four different cone photoreceptor types (Nawrocki et al., 1985), each distributed differently across the retina.
evidence: The manuscript cites Nawrocki et al., 1985 for the number of photoreceptor types.

claim: UV photoreceptors are densest in the ventro-temporal retina (area temporalis ventralis) of zebrafish.
source: UV photoreceptors are densest in the ventro-temporal retina (area temporalis ventralis), whereas the red, green, and blue photoreceptors cover more central retinal regions (Zimmermann et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Zimmermann et al., 2018 for photoreceptor distribution.

claim: Red, green, and blue photoreceptors cover more central retinal regions in zebrafish.
source: UV photoreceptors are densest in the ventro-temporal retina (area temporalis ventralis), whereas the red, green, and blue photoreceptors cover more central retinal regions (Zimmermann et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Zimmermann et al., 2018 for photoreceptor distribution.

claim: In humans, optokinetic responses are strongest in the central visual field.
source: In humans, optokinetic responses are strongest in the central visual field (Howard and Ohmi, 1984).
evidence: The manuscript cites Howard and Ohmi, 1984 for human OKR characteristics.

claim: In humans, lower visual field locations of the stimulus evoke stronger OKR than upper visual field locations.
source: Furthermore, lower visual field locations of the stimulus evoke stronger OKR than upper visual field locations, which likely represents an adaptation to the rich optic flow information available from the structures on the ground in the natural environments of primates (Murasugi and Howard, 1989; Hafed and Chen, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Murasugi and Howard, 1989 and Hafed and Chen, 2016 for this observation.

claim: The lower visual field preference in human OKR likely represents an adaptation to the rich optic flow information available from structures on the ground in natural primate environments.
source: Furthermore, lower visual field locations of the stimulus evoke stronger OKR than upper visual field locations, which likely represents an adaptation to the rich optic flow information available from the structures on the ground in the natural environments of primates (Murasugi and Howard, 1989; Hafed and Chen, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript provides an evolutionary interpretation of the observation.

claim: Small-field stimuli are effective in driving OKR in humans.
source: Despite the common notion that OKR is a whole-field gaze stabilisation behaviour, our results show that the OKR can be driven effectively by moving stimuli that cover only small parts of the spherical surface (e.g. a half-maximum OKR gain is observed for a stimulus that covers 25% of the spherical surface). In humans, small-field stimuli are effective in driving OKR as well, and the optokinetic drive and motion percept varies for central and peripheral retinal locations, with central stimulus locations eliciting stronger optokinetic drive (Howard and Ohmi, 1984; Brandt et al., 1973).
evidence: The manuscript cites Howard and Ohmi, 1984 and Brandt et al., 1973 for human small-field OKR.

claim: In humans, central stimulus locations elicit stronger optokinetic drive than peripheral locations.
source: In humans, small-field stimuli are effective in driving OKR as well, and the optokinetic drive and motion percept varies for central and peripheral retinal locations, with central stimulus locations eliciting stronger optokinetic drive (Howard and Ohmi, 1984; Brandt et al., 1973).
evidence: The manuscript cites Howard and Ohmi, 1984 and Brandt et al., 1973 for this observation.

claim: Zebrafish react most strongly to lateral, nearly equatorial stimuli.
source: However, zebrafish react most strongly to lateral, nearly equatorial stimuli, consistent with previously reported spatial densities of red, green, and blue photoreceptors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: The two eyes of zebrafish are less yoked than previously thought.
source: We find that the two eyes are less yoked than previously thought and that spatial frequency tuning is similar across visual field positions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Spatial frequency tuning is similar across visual field positions in zebrafish.
source: We find that the two eyes are less yoked than previously thought and that spatial frequency tuning is similar across visual field positions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Motion vision circuits in zebrafish are anisotropic.
source: Our results demonstrate that motion vision circuits in zebrafish are anisotropic, and preferentially monitor areas with putative behavioural relevance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main conclusion.

claim: Motion vision circuits in zebrafish preferentially monitor areas with putative behavioural relevance.
source: Our results demonstrate that motion vision circuits in zebrafish are anisotropic, and preferentially monitor areas with putative behavioural relevance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main conclusion.

claim: The spherical arena uses 232 LED tiles with 64 LEDs each.
source: We arranged 232 LED tiles with 64 LEDs each across a spherical arena, such that 14,484 LEDs (green dots) covered nearly the entire visual field.
evidence: Figure 1c caption provides specific numbers of tiles and LEDs.

claim: The spherical arena covers 85-90% of the visual field for stimulus presentation.
source: Across 85-90% of the visual field, we can then present horizontally moving bar patterns of different location, frequency and size to evoke OKR.
evidence: Figure 1h caption states the coverage percentage.

claim: The distance between most adjacent LED pairs is smaller than the photoreceptor spacing in the larval retina.
source: The distance between most of the adjacent LED pairs is smaller than the photoreceptor spacing in the larval retina (Haug et al., 2010; Tappeiner et al., 2012), resulting in a good spatial resolution across the majority of the spherical arena surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, see Materials and methods section on resolution).
evidence: The manuscript cites Haug et al., 2010 and Tappeiner et al., 2012 for photoreceptor spacing.

claim: The LED spacing results in good spatial resolution across the majority of the spherical arena surface.
source: The distance between most of the adjacent LED pairs is smaller than the photoreceptor spacing in the larval retina (Haug et al., 2010; Tappeiner et al., 2012), resulting in a good spatial resolution across the majority of the spherical arena surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, see Materials and methods section on resolution).
evidence: The manuscript infers good resolution from the LED spacing relative to photoreceptor spacing.

claim: Horizontally moving vertical bars reliably elicit OKR in zebrafish larvae.
source: Horizontally moving vertical bars reliably elicit OKR in zebrafish larvae (Beck et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites Beck et al., 2004 for this observation.

claim: The stimulus used rotated clock- and counter-clockwise with a sinusoidal velocity pattern (velocity amplitude 12.5 degree/s, frequency of the velocity envelope 0.1 Hz, spatial frequency 0.06 cycles/degree).
source: We used a stimulus which rotated clock- and counter-clockwise with a sinusoidal velocity pattern (velocity amplitude 12.5 degree/s, frequency of the velocity envelope 0.1 Hz, spatial frequency 0.06 cycles/degree, Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific parameters of the stimulus used.

claim: Small stimuli are sufficient to elicit reliable OKR, although gains are low if stimuli appear in a disfavoured part of the visual field.
source: Even small stimuli are sufficient to elicit reliable OKR, although gains are low if stimuli appear in a disfavoured part of the visual field.
evidence: Figure 2c caption describes the observation with example traces.

claim: OKR gain is significantly higher for lateral stimulus locations and lower across the rest of the visual field.
source: OKR gain is significantly higher for lateral stimulus locations and lower across the rest of the visual field.
evidence: Figure 3b-d caption states this main finding.

claim: The spatial distribution of OKR gains is well explained by the bimodal sum of two von-Mises Fisher distributions.
source: The spatial distribution of OKR gains is well explained by the bimodal sum of two von-Mises Fisher distributions.
evidence: Figure 3b-d caption describes the statistical model fit.

claim: OKR was strongest for stimuli near an azimuth of −82.5 degrees and an elevation of 5.1 degrees for the left side.
source: OKR was strongest for stimuli near an azimuth of −82.5 degrees and an elevation of 5.1 degrees for the left side (in body-centred coordinates), as well as 81.7 and 1.6 degrees for the right side – slightly rostral of the lateral meridian, and slightly above the equator.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific coordinates for maximum OKR gain.

claim: OKR was strongest for stimuli near an azimuth of 81.7 degrees and an elevation of 1.6 degrees for the right side.
source: OKR was strongest for stimuli near an azimuth of −82.5 degrees and an elevation of 5.1 degrees for the left side (in body-centred coordinates), as well as 81.7 and 1.6 degrees for the right side – slightly rostral of the lateral meridian, and slightly above the equator.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific coordinates for maximum OKR gain.

claim: In the nasal visual field (binocular overlap) the OKR gain was relatively high, but still lower than for lateral visual field locations.
source: In the nasal visual field (binocular overlap) the OKR gain was relatively high, but still lower than for lateral visual field locations.
evidence: The manuscript describes OKR gain in the binocular region.

claim: Control experiments showed no significant difference in OKR gain when additional dark triangular patches were present.
source: We thus performed control experiments comparing the OKR gain evoked by a stimulus in a densely covered part of the arena to the OKR gain evoked by same stimulus, but in the presence of additional dark triangular patches (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a). We found no significant difference in OKR gain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c, t-test, p>0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports results of control experiments with statistical test.

claim: Control experiments showed no significant difference in OKR gain when a dark shape mimicking the front 'keel' of the arena was present.
source: Additionally, we performed another series of control experiments using a dark shape mimicking the dark structural elements, the front 'keel' of the arena (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b). Again, we found no difference in OKR gain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c, t-test, p>0.05), and thus ruled out that position dependence data was corrupted by incomplete LED coverage.
evidence: The manuscript reports results of control experiments with statistical test.

claim: Animals maintained similar median horizontal eye positions even for the most peripheral stimulus positions.
source: We found that animals instead maintained similar median horizontal eye positions (e.g. left eye: −83.7 ± 1.8 degrees, right eye: 80.3 ± 1.9 degrees, average median ± standard deviation of medians, n = 7 fish, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) even for the most peripheral stimulus positions.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements of eye positions.

claim: When upright, azimuths and fish-centred elevations of the peaks of the best fits to data were −78.7° and 8.2° for the left eye, as well as 81.8° and 3.1° for the right eye.
source: When upright, azimuths and fish-centred elevations of the peaks of the best fits to data were −78.7° and 8.2° for the left eye, as well as 81.8° and 3.1° for the right eye.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements from upright fish.

claim: When inverted, azimuths and fish-centred elevations of the peaks of the best fits to data were −88.0° and 1.6° for the left eye, as well as 82.8° and −15.5° for the right eye.
source: When inverted, −88.0° and 1.6° for the left eye, as well as 82.8° and −15.5° for the right eye.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements from inverted fish.

claim: A permutation test confirmed that fish preferred upward (in the environmental reference frame) rather than dorsalward elevations (p<0.05).
source: This test confirmed that fish preferred upward (in the environmental reference frame) rather than dorsalward elevations (p<0.05, Source code 1E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports results of a permutation test with p-value.

claim: For both upside-up and upside-down embedding the eyes were inclined by an average of about four degrees towards the dorsum.
source: However, time-lapse frontal microscopy images (Materials and methods) ruled this out, since for both upside-up and upside-down embedding the eyes were inclined by an average of about four degrees towards the dorsum (3.5 ± 1.0° for the left eye, 4.9 ± 0.8° for the right eye, mean ± s.e.m., Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements of eye inclination.

claim: Eye-, head-, or body-centred reference frames are not sufficient to fully explain the observed optokinetic stimulus location preferences.
source: Eye-, head-, or body-centred reference frames are therefore not sufficient to fully explain the observed optokinetic stimulus location preferences.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the upside-down experiments.

claim: The stimulus location preference is additionally related to the environmental reference frame.
source: Instead, the stimulus location preference is additionally related to the environmental reference frame, suggesting that the behavioural relevance of our motion stimuli depends on their environmental elevation positions.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the experimental results.

claim: Almost all stimuli were presented monocularly – that is, in a position visible to only one of the two laterally located eyes.
source: Almost all stimuli were presented monocularly – that is, in a position visible to only one of the two laterally located eyes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the stimulus presentation method.

claim: Without exception, zebrafish larvae responded with yoked movements of both the stimulated and unstimulated eye.
source: Without exception, zebrafish larvae responded with yoked movements of both the stimulated and unstimulated eye.
evidence: The manuscript reports a consistent observation across all experiments.

claim: Yoking indices were significantly different between the regular monocular setup (YI≈0.2) and the control setup (YI≈0.7) containing the black surface on the side of the unstimulated eye.
source: Yoking indices (YI) were significantly different between the regular monocular setup (YI≈0.2) and the control setup (YI≈0.7) containing the black surface on the side of the unstimulated eye, confirming that yoking indices had been affected by reflections (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, an index of 1 indicating completely monocular eye movements, an index of 0 perfectly conjugate eye movements/yoking).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative comparison of yoking indices.

claim: Previously reported yoking partially depends on reflections of the stimulus pattern at the glass-to-air or water-to-air interface in the spherical setup and other commonly used stimulus arenas.
source: This suggests that previously reported yoking partially depends on reflections of the stimulus pattern at the glass-to-air or water-to-air interface in our spherical setup and other commonly used stimulus arenas.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the control experiment results.

claim: Yoking was much reduced (YI≈0.3) if the non-stimulated eye saw a stationary grating instead of the white or black shields (YI≈0.1) or a binocular motion stimulus (YI≈0).
source: This experiment showed that yoking was much reduced (YI≈0.3) if the non-stimulated eye saw a stationary grating (i) instead of the white or black shields (ii-iii, YI≈0.1) or a binocular motion stimulus (YI≈0) (Figure 3—figure supplement 5g–h, p<0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative results from control experiments.

claim: The OKR appears to be symmetric between both eyes across individuals, although individual animals oftentimes have a dominant eye.
source: Across individuals, the OKR appears to be symmetric between both eyes, although individual animals oftentimes have a dominant eye.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings on lateralization.

claim: For each stimulus location and eye, the highest OKR gain was observed at a spatial frequency of 0.03 to 0.05 cycles/degree.
source: For each stimulus location and eye, the highest OKR gain was observed at a spatial frequency of 0.03 to 0.05 cycles/degree (Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the optimal spatial frequency range.

claim: No strong modulation of frequency dependence by stimulus location was observed.
source: We did not observe any strong modulation of frequency dependence by stimulus location.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of a location effect on frequency tuning.

claim: OKR gain increased sigmoidally with the logarithm of stimulus size.
source: In line with many other psychophysical processes, OKR gain increased sigmoidally with the logarithm of stimulus size (Figure 5e, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between stimulus size and OKR gain.

claim: Weak OKR behaviour was already observable in response to very small stimuli of 0.8% (solid angle or 'stimulus diameter' of 10.4°).
source: Weak OKR behaviour was already observable in response to very small stimuli of 0.8% (solid angle or 'stimulus diameter' of 10.4°), and reached half-maximum performance at a stimulus size of roughly 25% (solid angle: 120°).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements of stimulus size effects.

claim: OKR reached half-maximum performance at a stimulus size of roughly 25% (solid angle: 120°).
source: Weak OKR behaviour was already observable in response to very small stimuli of 0.8% (solid angle or 'stimulus diameter' of 10.4°), and reached half-maximum performance at a stimulus size of roughly 25% (solid angle: 120°).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements of stimulus size effects.

claim: The left eye responded more strongly to ipsilateral than contralateral stimuli (ANOVA, p<0.05).
source: Specifically, the left eye responded more strongly to ipsilateral than contralateral stimuli (ANOVA, p<0.05), whereas the right eye did not (ANOVA, p>0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results for stimulus location effects.

claim: The right eye did not respond more strongly to ipsilateral than contralateral stimuli (ANOVA, p>0.05).
source: Specifically, the left eye responded more strongly to ipsilateral than contralateral stimuli (ANOVA, p<0.05), whereas the right eye did not (ANOVA, p>0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results for stimulus location effects.

claim: For green, blue, and especially red receptors, the visual space location in which OKR gain is maximal coincides with a retinal region of near-maximum photoreceptor density.
source: For green, blue, and especially red receptors, the visual space location in which OKR gain is maximal (cf, Figure 3e) coincides with a retinal region of near-maximum photoreceptor density (white ring in Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript compares OKR gain maps to photoreceptor density maps.

claim: For ultraviolet receptors, there is no strong correlation between photoreceptor density and OKR gain.
source: For ultraviolet receptors (Figure 6b), there is no strong correlation between photoreceptor density and OKR gain.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of correlation for UV receptors.

claim: The average eye position was located horizontally at −84.8 ± 6.2 degrees azimuth for the left and 80.1 ± 6.5 deg for the right eye (mean ±st.dev., n = 7 fish).
source: To register our OKR gain data onto the photoreceptor density maps, we took the average eye position into account, which was located horizontally at −84.8 ± 6.2 degrees azimuth for the left and 80.1 ± 6.5 deg for the right eye (mean ±st.dev., n = 7 fish), and vertically at 3.5 ± 3.2 degrees elevation for the left and 4.9 ± 2.7 deg for the right eye (n = 10 fish).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements of eye positions.

claim: The average eye position was located vertically at 3.5 ± 3.2 degrees elevation for the left and 4.9 ± 2.7 deg for the right eye (n = 10 fish).
source: To register our OKR gain data onto the photoreceptor density maps, we took the average eye position into account, which was located horizontally at −84.8 ± 6.2 degrees azimuth for the left and 80.1 ± 6.5 deg for the right eye (mean ±st.dev., n = 7 fish), and vertically at 3.5 ± 3.2 degrees elevation for the left and 4.9 ± 2.7 deg for the right eye (n = 10 fish).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements of eye positions.

claim: No significant shift in the position-dependence of maximum OKR gain was observed between groups of larvae at 5, 6, or 7 dpf of age.
source: We did not observe a significant shift in the position-dependence of maximum OKR gain between groups of larvae at 5, 6, or 7 dpf of age, consistent with the notion that retinal development is far advanced and the circuits governing OKR behaviour are stable at this developmental stage.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of age-dependent differences.

claim: Retinal development is far advanced and the circuits governing OKR behaviour are stable at 5-7 dpf developmental stage.
source: We did not observe a significant shift in the position-dependence of maximum OKR gain between groups of larvae at 5, 6, or 7 dpf of age, consistent with the notion that retinal development is far advanced and the circuits governing OKR behaviour are stable at this developmental stage.
evidence: The manuscript infers developmental stability from the lack of age effects.

claim: The spherical arena provides homogeneous light and contrast across the entire stimulation area.
source: In comparison to other feasible technical solutions, such as video projection setups, our spherical LED array stimulus setup provides homogeneous light and contrast across the entire stimulation area.
evidence: The manuscript describes an advantage of the LED arena design.

claim: Using the LED arena, stimulus design is much easier because stimulus warping and conditioning becomes unnecessary.
source: Thereby, stimulus design is much easier because stimulus warping and conditioning becomes unnecessary.
evidence: The manuscript describes a practical advantage of the design.

claim: When combined with calcium imaging in a scanning microscope, the use of LED arrays provides the advantage that the visual stimulus can be controlled with high temporal precision, fast enough to interlace visual stimuli and line scans.
source: When combined with calcium imaging in a scanning microscope, the use of LED arrays provides the additional advantage that the visual stimulus can be controlled with high temporal precision, fast enough to interlace visual stimuli and line scans.
evidence: The manuscript describes a technical advantage for imaging experiments.

claim: The spatial frequency tuning of zebrafish OKR is similar across retinal locations.
source: Our experiment on spatial frequency dependence further demonstrates that the spatial frequency tuning of zebrafish OKR is similar across retinal locations.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes a main finding.

claim: Photoreceptor density is not the limiting factor for OKR performance in the tested frequency range.
source: Since photoreceptors are not equally distributed across the retina, this result suggests that photoreceptor density is not the limiting factor for OKR performance in this frequency range.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the frequency tuning results.

claim: Almost no consistent, inter-individual asymmetries in OKR were observed between the left and right hemispheres of the visual field, other than those induced by external conditions.
source: We observed almost no consistent, inter-individual asymmetries in OKR between the left and right hemispheres of the visual field, other than those induced by external conditions.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings on lateralization.

claim: Individual fish show a wide and continuous range of biases towards either hemisphere.
source: Individual fish, however, show a wide and continuous range of biases towards either hemisphere.
evidence: The manuscript describes individual variability in lateralization.

claim: OKR gain was measured in larvae at 5–7 days post fertilisation (dpf) of age.
source: We measured OKR gain in larvae at 5–7 days post fertilisation (dpf) of age, whereas our data on photoreceptor densities corresponds to slightly older, 7–8 dpf larvae.
evidence: The manuscript specifies the age of larvae used.

claim: The zebrafish retina is well developed by five dpf.
source: Owing to their rapid development, zebrafish undergo noticeable morphological changes on this timescale, but the zebrafish retina itself is known to be well developed by five dpf (Avanesov and Malicki, 2010) and stable OKR behaviour is exhibited from then on.
evidence: The manuscript cites Avanesov and Malicki, 2010 for retinal development.

claim: Stable OKR behaviour is exhibited from five dpf onwards.
source: Owing to their rapid development, zebrafish undergo noticeable morphological changes on this timescale, but the zebrafish retina itself is known to be well developed by five dpf (Avanesov and Malicki, 2010) and stable OKR behaviour is exhibited from then on.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge.

claim: The qualitative match between red cone retinal photoreceptor densities and the stimulus position driving the highest OKR gains may provide a mechanistic bottom-up explanation of the gradual differences associated with OKR.
source: The qualitative match between red cone retinal photoreceptor densities and the stimulus position driving the highest OKR gains may provide a mechanistic bottom-up explanation of the gradual differences associated with OKR.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic interpretation.

claim: The correspondence of red photoreceptor density with the visual field map of OKR gain is consistent with the fact that the LEDs emit light at 568 nm peak power, which should have activated the red cones most.
source: The correspondence of red photoreceptor density with the visual field map of OKR gain is consistent with the fact that our LEDs emit light at 568 nm peak power, which should have activated the red cones most.
evidence: The manuscript relates LED spectrum to photoreceptor activation.

claim: The data is in agreement with observations in other species, that the OKR drive is strongest when the moving stimulus covers the central visual field.
source: Our data is also in agreement with observations in other species, that the OKR drive is strongest when the moving stimulus covers the central visual field (Murasugi and Howard, 1989; Shimizu et al., 2010; Howard and Ohmi, 1984).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies for comparison across species.

claim: Melanopsin-expressing ganglion cells contribute to form vision.
source: Recent studies suggest that melanopsin-expressing ganglion cells also contribute to form vision (Allen et al., 2019; Lucas et al., 2020), and melanopsins as well as a plethora of other opsins are expressed in the zebrafish retina and brain (Davies et al., 2015; Fontinha et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent studies on melanopsin function.

claim: Melanopsins and other opsins are expressed in the zebrafish retina and brain.
source: Recent studies suggest that melanopsin-expressing ganglion cells also contribute to form vision (Allen et al., 2019; Lucas et al., 2020), and melanopsins as well as a plethora of other opsins are expressed in the zebrafish retina and brain (Davies et al., 2015; Fontinha et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on opsin expression in zebrafish.

claim: It is possible that photoreception via opsin-expressing neurons in the inner retina contributes to zebrafish OKR.
source: It is therefore possible that photoreception via opsin-expressing neurons in the inner retina contributes to zebrafish OKR as well.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about alternative photoreceptive mechanisms.

claim: When animals were mounted upside-down, they still prefer stimulus locations just above the equator of the environment.
source: Interestingly, when animals were mounted upside-down, they still prefer stimulus locations just above the equator of the environment.
evidence: The manuscript reports a key finding from control experiments.

claim: The upside-down preference result cannot be explained by shifted resting vertical eye positions in the inverted animal.
source: This result cannot be explained by shifted resting vertical eye positions in the inverted animal, which we have measured.
evidence: The manuscript rules out one potential explanation.

claim: The upside-down preference could potentially be explained by multimodal integration, where body orientation appears to influence the preferred OKR stimulus locations via the vestibular system.
source: Instead, it could potentially be explained by multimodal integration, where body orientation appears to influence the preferred OKR stimulus locations via the vestibular system (Lafortune et al., 1990; Pettorossi et al., 2011; Zolotilina et al., 1995).
evidence: The manuscript proposes an alternative explanation with citations.

claim: The unequal distribution of OKR gains across the visual field might be related to the optic flow statistics that naturally occur in the habitats of larval zebrafish.
source: Furthermore, it seems possible that the unequal distribution of OKR gains across the visual field is related to the optic flow statistics that naturally occur in the habitats of larval zebrafish (Zimmermann et al., 2018; Arunachalam et al., 2013; Engeszer et al., 2007; Parichy, 2015; Spence et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript proposes an ecological explanation with citations.

claim: For the optomotor response, the underlying circuits prefer stimulus locations in the lower temporal visual field to drive forward optomotor swimming.
source: For another stabilisation behaviour of zebrafish, the optomotor response (Orger et al., 2008), we have recently shown that the underlying circuits prefer stimulus locations in the lower temporal visual field to drive forward optomotor swimming (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a recent study on optomotor response.

claim: The optokinetic and the optomotor response are preferentially driven by different regions in the visual field.
source: Therefore, the optokinetic and the optomotor response are preferentially driven by different regions in the visual field, suggesting that they occur in response to different types of optic flow patterns in natural habitats.
evidence: The manuscript infers functional differences from spatial preferences.

claim: Both the optokinetic and the optomotor response (OKR, OMR) are thought to be mediated by the pretectum.
source: Both the optokinetic and the optomotor response (OKR, OMR) are thought to be mediated by the pretectum (Kubo et al., 2014; Naumann et al., 2016), and we therefore hypothesise that circuits mediating OKR and OMR segregate within the pretectum and form neuronal ensembles with mostly different receptive field centre locations.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on pretectal mediation of these behaviors.

claim: Circuits mediating OKR and OMR segregate within the pretectum and form neuronal ensembles with mostly different receptive field centre locations.
source: Both the optokinetic and the optomotor response (OKR, OMR) are thought to be mediated by the pretectum (Kubo et al., 2014; Naumann et al., 2016), and we therefore hypothesise that circuits mediating OKR and OMR segregate within the pretectum and form neuronal ensembles with mostly different receptive field centre locations.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a hypothesis about pretectal organization.

source: Animal experiments were performed in accordance with licenses granted by local government authorities (Regierungspräsidium Tübingen) in accordance with German federal law and Baden-Württemberg state law.

source: We used mitfa-/- animals (5–7 dpf) for the experiments, because this strain lacks skin pigmentation that could interfere with eye tracking.
evidence: The manuscript explains the rationale for using this genetic strain.

source: One report suggests that mitfa-/- animals show different optomotor responses than wildtype animals (Stowers et al., 2017), so it is possible that optokinetic responses investigated here are also modulated by this genetic background.

claim: The overall layout of the spherical arena was optimised to contain the near maximum number of LED tiles that can be driven by the hardware controllers (232 out of a possible 240).
source: The overall layout of the spherical arena was optimised to contain the near maximum number of LED tiles that can be driven by our hardware controllers (232 out of a possible 240), and arrange them with minimal gaps in between.
evidence: The manuscript describes the design optimization.

claim: The electronic and software architecture of stimulus control has originally been designed by Reiser and Dickinson, 2008.

source: However, larval zebrafish have poor visual acuity, since each retina of their tiny eyes only contains about 10,000 photoreceptors (Zimmermann et al., 2018), corresponding to about 1–2 red-green double cone photoreceptors per square degree (Haug et al., 2010; Tappeiner et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on photoreceptor numbers and density.
